newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open narrowly mixed after Christmas.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open narrowly mixed after Christmas.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened barely changed in quiet trade on Thursday, the day after Christmas when the market closed for the holiday.
With no economic data due and many participants extending their holiday, analysts said they expected trading to be very quiet and narrow-ranged.

"Very tired and narrow-ranged is the only way to say it, much like we got on the 24th, partly because there's no data and partly because a lot of people are taking the day off," said Astrid Adolfson, MCM MoneyWatch financial economist.
There was no trading in Europe overnight to lend the market early direction since markets were closed there, too, for Christmas.
"There's no incentive to do anything either way," said Adolfson. "Tomorrow there is some data so the hope is we'll get a little activity tomorrow morning."

The government will release weekly data on new and continuing jobless claims on Friday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. Economists polled by Reuters estimate those claims slipped to 346,000 in the latest week from 351,000 a week earlier.
November durable goods orders data are also due on Friday. Economists polled by Reuters expect those to be up 0.1 percent after a 0.3 percent October rise.
Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International, said technicals would probably dominate trade on Thursday.
Rupert said MMS looks for an eventual move up through 113-21 on the March T-bond contract, targeting the 114-06 area.
"We see support around 113 and below that, near 112-25," she said.
Otherwise, the market should trade very quietly, Rupert said, with no major movements in either direction.
"There's no data coming out so there won't be any fundamental directional signals," she said.
In early trade, the 30-year bond firmed to 99 even, up 4/32, its yield at 6.58 percent.
Ten-year notes were up 3/32 to 101-7/32, yielding 6.33 percent.
Five-year notes were up 1/32 to 100 even, yielding 6.12 percent. Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-27/32, yielding 5.83 percent.
Three-, six- and year-bill rates were each down one basis point to 4.94 percent, 5.05 percent and 5.19 percent, respectively.
